questions.q: What are the defining traits of a REST API?
options: Resource-based URLs, standard HTTP verbs like GET and POST, and typically JSON payloads
A formal WSDL contract and XML-only payloads
It can only be used for event-driven integrations
It requires a MID Server for every call
questions.explain: REST organizes around resources addressed by URLs, acted on with standard HTTP verbs, with JSON as the typical payload format.

questions.q: What is a WSDL, and which protocol does it belong to?
options: A JSON schema used to validate REST payloads
A ServiceNow table used to log integration errors
A formal, machine-readable contract document describing a SOAP service's operations, parameters, and response shapes
An authentication token format used by webhooks
questions.explain: WSDL (Web Services Description Language) is the formal contract that defines exactly what a SOAP service offers and expects.

questions.q: Why is SOAP still common in industries like finance, government, and telecom, despite being more rigid and verbose than REST?
options: SOAP is actually simpler to hand-write than REST
SOAP cannot be replaced by REST under any circumstances for technical reasons
REST does not support financial or government data of any kind
Those industries often run core systems built decades ago, long before REST existed, and were never rewritten just because REST became fashionable
questions.explain: Legacy core systems in regulated industries often predate REST entirely, and a SOAP interface (with its WSDL contract) may be the only one available.

questions.q: What actually distinguishes event-driven integration from a typical REST or SOAP call?
options: Event-driven integration never uses HTTP at all
It's defined by who initiates and when — a notification is pushed the instant something happens, rather than being requested on a polling loop — not by JSON vs. XML
Event-driven integration is just another name for SOAP
It only applies to integrations involving a MID Server
questions.explain: Event-driven integration is a category defined by behavior (pushed immediately vs. polled on demand), and a webhook is often still an HTTP-based, REST-shaped call underneath.

questions.q: Why does a working ServiceNow integration developer need to be comfortable with REST, SOAP, and event-driven patterns, rather than just REST?
options: Because SOAP is always faster than REST
Because ServiceNow does not actually support REST integrations
Because the external system's existing architecture, not the developer's preference, dictates which pattern a given integration must use
Because event-driven integration has replaced both REST and SOAP entirely
questions.explain: A legacy SOAP-only system or an event-streaming platform will force a specific pattern regardless of what's fashionable or preferred — the developer has to be able to meet the external system where it is.
